kurz: Why sorting rules such as value, size, momentum and quality have delivered excess returns over decades, why little of this reaches ETF investors, and which findings survive the debate on replicability.

bloecke.md:
A factor is a sorting rule and is neither a share nor a fund. All the shares in a market are ranked by a characteristic, such as book value per euro of market value, company size, the price trend of recent months or operating profitability. The top third is bought, the bottom third is sold short, and the return difference is measured over decades. If this systematically leaves a return that cannot be explained by market risk, researchers speak of a [[Factor premium|factor premium]].

In 1993 Fama and French extended the CAPM by adding size and value, Carhart did so in 1997 by adding momentum, and Fama/French in 2015 by adding profitability (RMW) and investment behaviour (CMA). Their practical use lies first of all in measurement. A regression of fund returns on these factors makes it possible to separate which part is a characteristic premium that can be replicated cheaply and which part is due to genuine skill on the part of the manager.

bloecke.formel: r_Fund − r_f = α + b × (r_Market − r_f) + s × SMB + h × HML + w × WML + ε
bloecke.erklaerung: Carhart regression on monthly returns. The coefficients are called factor loadings and indicate how strongly a fund depends on a factor. Alpha is the return that remains after that.
variablen: residual return that no factor explains
bloecke.beispiel: A pure long-short value portfolio would have h = 1. A long-only value ETF typically has b close to 1 and h between 0.3 and 0.5. It therefore receives only a third to a half of the factor effect.

bloecke.md:
## How the factors are calculated

Kenneth French deliberately constructs the factors according to mechanical rules. The boundary between small and large companies is the NYSE median, and the boundaries for the respective characteristic lie at the 30th and 70th NYSE percentiles. The calculation is value-weighted in 2×3 sorts. HML is the average of Small Value and Big Value minus the average of Small Growth and Big Growth. Momentum measures the price trend from month −12 to −2. The most recent month is left out, because short-term price reversals predominate over this period, and the sort is renewed monthly.

The following premiums are calculated from the raw data of the Kenneth French database up to July 2026, geometric and annualised. The t-statistic indicates how reliably a premium differs from zero. From about 2.0 upwards, it is considered significant by classical convention.

bloecke.titel: Factors of the standard model (USA, long-short, before costs)

bloecke.md: After the market, momentum has the largest premium, higher than that of value. The size factor, which regularly appears in product brochures as the small-cap premium, cannot by contrast be statistically distinguished from zero over a hundred years. Calculated arithmetically, the HML premium would be 4.26% instead of 3.59%. The difference of 0.67 percentage points is purely a volatility deduction and not a return that accrues to an investor.

Every figure in the table comes from a long-short portfolio without trading costs, taxes or short-selling restrictions, which is re-sorted monthly for momentum and annually at the end of June for SMB, HML, RMW and CMA. It does not describe a fund that you can buy. Every step from these values to a real portfolio costs return.

bloecke.titel: Factor premiums by decade, USA (% p.a., geometric)
bloecke.unter: No factor delivers steady returns; each has entire decades with a negative premium, including the market. The last group of bars covers 2020 to July 2026.

bloecke.md: Factor premiums do not accrue evenly like interest; they run in cycles lasting decades. Of all rolling ten-year windows since 1926, 35.0% were negative for SMB, 20.5% for momentum, 14.3% for HML and 13.5% for the market premium. Even over twenty years, SMB is negative in 19.5% of all windows, momentum in 9.3% and HML in 7.4%. Since 1964, SMB has been positive in as many calendar years as it has been negative, which corresponds to a random result. HML was positive in 56% of years, momentum in 71% and the market in 73%.

bloecke.titel: Distance of the HML factor from its previous high, 1963-2026 (%)
bloecke.unter: After the high of December 2006 the factor fell, and by July 2026 it had still not regained this high.

bloecke.md:
The cumulative HML factor reached its high in December 2006 and lost 57.8% by September 2020. This was the deepest value setback since 1926. For the years 2007 to 2020, the result is −5.67% p.a., or −55.8% cumulatively.

Since 2021 the factor has been recovering, by +8.71% p.a. up to July 2026, or +59.4% cumulatively. The recovery rests on two exceptionally strong years (2021 +22.2%, 2022 +31.7%) and was interrupted by two loss-making years (2023 −11.1%, 2024 −7.0%). Nevertheless, in July 2026 the factor was still around 30% below its 2006 level, and had thus been below its high for 19.6 years.

These figures apply to the long-short portfolio. A value ETF fell much less far behind, because it participated in market performance through its market beta. The factor only measures the difference between value and growth and not the performance of a portfolio.

## Momentum and crash risk

With the momentum factor, losses are rare, but when they come they are sudden. In 2009 the factor lost 52.8% in total, 34.4% of it in April alone, and 49.4% cumulatively from March to May. In 1932 it lost 45.6% in July and 52.6% in August. The maximum drawdown from June 1932 to September 1939 was 78.4% and was only made good in December 1956, after around 24.5 years.

The crashes follow a recurring pattern. After a crash, the shares with the largest price losses are on the short side. If the market turns upwards amid high volatility, these shares rise particularly strongly. Daniel and Moskowitz show that such phases are partly predictable and that a momentum variant scaled by volatility roughly doubles alpha and the Sharpe ratio. Standard momentum indices do not use this technique.

bloecke.unter: The annual return of −52.8% arose almost entirely in three months, when the market rose again after the low in March.

bloecke.md:
## Size and quality

The size factor is a special case, because the premium has disappeared since its publication. From 1994 to July 2026, SMB delivered −0.29% p.a., since 1981 −0.21% p.a. and since 2021 −5.08% p.a. The high of July 1983 has not been regained since. This does not make small caps a wrong decision, but they do not automatically come with a premium.

The quality factors appear to be the most robust. Novy-Marx showed in 2013 that gross profitability per unit of assets predicts future returns about as well as the book-to-market ratio and significantly improves value strategies. Since 1963, RMW has delivered 2.81% p.a. with a volatility of only 7.9%, which gives it the calmest path of all the factors after CMA. For their broader definition of quality, made up of profitability, growth and safety, Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen find significant risk-adjusted returns in the USA and in a global sample of 24 countries including the USA.

For portfolio construction, the size of the premiums matters less than their independence from one another. HML and momentum have a monthly correlation of −0.19, HML and the market −0.21. This is what makes several factors useful. Only HML and CMA are so strongly correlated, at 0.68, that Fama and French themselves consider HML largely redundant in the five-factor model.

## How robust the findings are

Given the hundreds of published factors, Harvey, Liu and Zhu consider a t-hurdle of 3.0 instead of 1.96 to be appropriate, because patterns can be found in any data set if you search long enough. Hou, Xue and Zhang replicate 447 anomalies. Even at t > 1.96, 64% of them are insignificant, and at t > 3.0 the figure is 85%. The main reason is that the original studies gave equal weight to micro-caps that are hardly tradable in practice.

Other studies come to more favourable results. Using a hierarchical Bayesian approach, Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen show that the majority of factors can be replicated and grouped into a few themes, and that they hold up in 93 countries. Baltussen, Swinkels and van Vliet confirm 24 factor premiums over 217 years in equities, bonds, commodities and currencies. What is disputed, therefore, is less whether premiums exist than how large they will be in future and after costs.

A third finding is undisputed, namely that premiums shrink after publication. For 97 predictors, McLean and Pontiff measure 26% less return outside the original sample and 58% less after publication. Momentum follows the same pattern. From 1963 to 1993 the factor delivered 9.93% p.a., from 1994 to July 2026 still 3.06% and since 2000 only 0.82%.

bloecke.titel: Value premium from factor to portfolio (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: The order of magnitude of each step is documented. The chain as a whole is an estimate and neither a measurement nor a forecast.

bloecke.md: This order of magnitude is consistent with direct measurements. Chen and Velikov work through 204 long-short anomalies after bid-ask spreads, the publication effect and modern trading technology, and arrive at an average of 4 basis points a month, around 0.5% a year. The best reach 10 basis points. For smart beta indices, Huang, Song and Xiang measure around 3% p.a. excess return in the backtest before the launch of the associated ETF, and −0.5% to −1% p.a. afterwards. They attribute this to data mining in index construction and not to capacity constraints.

bloecke.titel: Factor ETFs in Germany (examples, not a recommendation; as of September 2026)
zeilen: iShares Edge MSCI World Momentum Factor
iShares Edge MSCI World Value Factor
iShares Edge MSCI World Quality Factor

bloecke.md: The extra cost of 0.11 to 0.21 percentage points is the smallest item here. Four other reasons weigh more heavily. First, a [[Smart beta|smart beta]] ETF is long-only. Market beta determines most of the return, and typically a third to a half of the pure factor remains. Second, each index provider defines the factor differently. MSCI Value Weighted, Enhanced Value and Prime Value are three different portfolios with noticeably different returns. Third, capping, liquidity and capacity rules distort the weights. Fourth, all turnover incurs costs for spread and market impact that do not occur in the academic factor.

Reallocations within the fund are tax-neutral for the investor. Even a factor ETF with 30% annual turnover does not trigger any tax for them. Your own switch, by contrast, is expensive. When you swap the value ETF for a momentum ETF after a weak phase, gains are realised. These are subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%, on 70% of the gain, because a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% applies to equity funds under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). Effectively, that is 18.46%. With a book gain of €10,000, €1,846 is then missing that would otherwise have remained invested. If a factor bet is not held over a full cycle, the investor bears the costs without receiving the premium.

First, the premium is confused with the product return. HML's 3.59% applies to a long-short portfolio without costs, not to an ETF.

Second, investors buy in after good factor years. This is the pattern measured by the study on smart beta backtests. The flattering back-calculation attracts money, after which the excess return turns negative.

Third, factors are combined without checking their overlap. Value, quality and low volatility in the same portfolio often diversify less than the three names suggest. HML and CMA, for example, have a correlation of 0.68.

All the premiums mentioned are based on US data, because only there do clean series going back to 1926 exist. For Europe, Japan and emerging markets, the histories are shorter and the premiums different. Fama and French themselves point out that local factors explain returns better than global ones. Baltussen and colleagues see the premiums confirmed internationally, but in less liquid markets the deduction for trading costs is larger. A world factor ETF in a German portfolio therefore contains the factors of many markets and also bears their implementation costs.

mitnehmen: Factors are sorting rules and not products; between HML's 3.59% on paper and the portfolio statement lie the dilution from long-only construction, the decline of the premium after its publication, trading costs and the TER.
Value, momentum and profitability are well documented, whereas the size premium has disappeared since 1994, at −0.29% p.a., and is not statistically significant over 100 years.
Long weak phases are the norm; for HML 14.3% of all ten-year windows are negative, for SMB 35.0%, and 19.6 years after its 2006 high, value is still below it.
Of the factors other than the market, momentum has the highest raw premium and the most severe crashes, with −34.4% in a single month (April 2009) and −78.4% in its largest drawdown.

After costs, the difference from a broad market index is realistically between about −1 and +0.5 percentage points a year, and for investors who cannot hold out through long weak phases, the low-cost market index is the better choice.

begriffe.text: Excess return of a long-short portfolio sorted by a characteristic that cannot be explained by market risk. It is calculated without costs and taxes.
Abbreviation for High Minus Low. The factor buys shares with a high book-to-market ratio (value) and sells growth shares short. The premium is 3.59% p.a. (USA, 1926-2026).

Abbreviation for Small Minus Big. The factor measures the return of shares with a small market capitalisation minus that of shares with a large market capitalisation. Over 100 years the premium is 1.42% p.a., but it is not significant and has been negative since 1994.

Abbreviation for Winners Minus Losers. The factor buys the price winners of months −12 to −2 and sells the losers short. Of the factors other than the market, it has the highest premium and the highest crash risk.
Regression coefficient indicating how strongly a fund's return depends on a factor. A value of 1 corresponds to the full factor, and long-only ETFs usually reach 0.3 to 0.5.
Marketing term for rule-based indices that deviate from market capitalisation weighting in order to capture factors. They are long-only, so the factor effect is heavily diluted.
